title: Concurrency in OO Design
summary: Multiple threads, one object. Learn why shared mutable state breaks designs, and how locks, double-checked locking, and immutability fix it.

blocks.markdown:
**Concurrency** is multiple threads running at once, possibly interleaving their steps on the same objects. Good OO design assumes one thread touches an object at a time — concurrency breaks that assumption.

- Shared **mutable** (changeable) state is the root cause of almost every concurrency bug.
- Fixes: **locks** (block other threads), or **immutability** (nothing to corrupt).
- LLD interviews test this on Singletons, counters, and shared resource classes (booking seats, rate limiters).

blocks.subTitle: Core vocabulary
blocks.markdown:
Terms used throughout this topic.

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Race condition | Outcome depends on thread timing |
| Critical section | Code touching shared state |
| Mutual exclusion | Only one thread in at a time |

Everything below is a way to protect the critical section.

A single-threaded design only has to be logically correct. The moment two threads call methods on the **same object**, correctness also depends on **timing** — and most designs never planned for that.

- **Shared mutable object**: one instance whose fields multiple threads read and write.
- If two threads update it at once, one thread's write can silently overwrite or corrupt the other's.
- This is why LLD interviews add "now make it thread-safe" to Singleton, counters, and booking systems.

blocks.subTitle: Race condition & critical section
blocks.markdown:
A **race condition** is a bug where the result depends on which thread happens to run first — the code is only correct for some interleavings.

- The **critical section** is the specific code that reads or writes shared state (e.g. `count = count + 1`).
- That single line is really read-modify-write; if two threads interleave inside it, one increment gets lost.
- A class is **thread-safe** only if every critical section is protected against this.

blocks.subTitle: Mutual exclusion
blocks.markdown:
**Mutual exclusion** is the guarantee that only one thread executes a critical section at a time — every other thread must wait its turn.

- Enforced with a **lock** (also called a mutex): a thread must acquire it before entering, and releases it on exit.
- If a second thread tries to acquire a held lock, it **blocks** (pauses) until the first releases it.
- Locks fix races but add cost: waiting threads do no useful work.

The standard fix is **synchronization**: wrap the critical section in a lock so mutual exclusion holds.

- Java's `synchronized` keyword on a method locks on the object itself — one thread runs the whole method at a time.
- Other languages use explicit lock objects (`Lock`, `Mutex`) acquired and released around the critical section only.
- Lock the **smallest** section that touches shared state — locking too much serializes threads that didn't need to wait.

A **Singleton** (see [creational-patterns](creational-patterns)) must hand out exactly one instance. With **lazy initialization** (create it on first use), two threads can both see "no instance yet" and each construct one — the one-instance guarantee breaks.

- This only shows up under concurrent first access — easy to miss in a single-threaded test.
- Three standard fixes exist, each with a different cost.

blocks.subTitle: Fix 1: eager initialization
blocks.markdown:
**Eager initialization** creates the instance at class-load time, before any thread can race for it.

- The runtime guarantees class loading happens once — so it's automatically thread-safe, no locks needed.
- Downside: the instance is built even if the app never uses it, wasting startup cost/memory.
- Good default when construction is cheap or the Singleton is always needed.

blocks.subTitle: Fix 2: synchronized method
blocks.markdown:
**Synchronized `getInstance()`** locks the whole method, so only one thread can check-and-create at a time.

- Correct and simple to write.
- Costly: every call acquires the lock, even the millionth call when the instance already exists and no race can happen anymore.
- That unnecessary locking on the common (already-created) path motivates the next fix.

blocks.subTitle: Fix 3: double-checked locking
blocks.markdown:
**Double-checked locking (DCL)** checks "is it null?" **before** locking, and again **after** locking, only creating the instance if it's still null.

- First check (no lock): skips locking entirely once the instance exists — fast path for nearly every call.
- Lock only guards the rare first-time creation window.
- Second check (inside the lock): catches the case where another thread created it while this one was waiting for the lock.

blocks.subTitle: Pseudocode: double-checked locking
blocks.markdown:
```text
class Singleton:
    static volatile instance = null
    static lock = new Lock()

    static method getInstance():
        if instance == null:            // 1st check, no lock — fast path
            lock.acquire()
            try:
                if instance == null:    // 2nd check, inside lock
                    instance = new Singleton()
            finally:
                lock.release()
        return instance
```
`volatile` stops a thread from seeing a half-built object — without it, DCL can still hand out a broken instance.

An **immutable object** can't change state after construction — every field is set once and never reassigned.

- No mutable state means no critical section, no race condition, and no lock ever needed.
- Multiple threads can read the same immutable object freely and safely, forever.
- The trade-off: any "change" must return a **new** object instead of modifying the old one.

blocks.subTitle: Pseudocode: immutable class
blocks.markdown:
```text
class Point:
    final x          // final — set once, never reassigned
    final y

    constructor(x, y):
        this.x = x
        this.y = y

    // "mutation" returns a new object; original is untouched
    method movedBy(dx, dy):
        return new Point(this.x + dx, this.y + dy)
```
Any thread holding a `Point` can read `x`/`y` with zero locking — it will never change.

Two different strategies for the same goal.

| | Locks/synchronization | Immutability |
|---|---|---|
| State | Mutable, guarded | None to guard |
| Cost | Waiting, deadlock risk | Extra object allocation |

Prefer immutability wherever the object's data doesn't truly need to change; reach for locks only for state that must mutate in place.

Most languages ship pre-built safe primitives so you don't hand-roll locks for common cases.

- **Thread-safe collections** (`ConcurrentHashMap`, `CopyOnWriteArrayList`) internally lock or partition so concurrent access can't corrupt them.
- **Atomic operations** (`AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet()`) perform read-modify-write as one indivisible hardware step — no lock needed for a single counter.
- Reach for these before writing custom locking; they're tested and usually faster.

blocks.sectionTitle: Designing for concurrency in interview problems
blocks.markdown:
Classic LLD problems make concurrency the whole point: two users must never book the same seat; a rate limiter must count requests correctly under load.

- Identify the shared mutable state first (a seat's status, a request counter) — that's what needs protecting.
- Then choose: lock around the update, or model it as immutable snapshots swapped atomically.
- See worked designs in [case-study-movie-booking](case-study-movie-booking) and [case-study-rate-limiter](case-study-rate-limiter).

Common mistakes:

- **Forgetting `volatile` in DCL.** Without it, a thread can read a reference to a half-constructed object — DCL silently breaks.
- **Synchronizing everything.** Locking whole classes "to be safe" serializes threads that never conflicted, killing throughput.
- **Assuming immutability is free.** It's simple to reason about, but every "change" allocates a new object — a real cost under heavy churn.

blocks.subTitle: What is a race condition
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What is a race condition?**

A bug where the outcome depends on the unpredictable timing of thread execution — the code only gives the right answer for some interleavings. Classic example: two threads both read a counter as 5, both increment, both write 6 — one increment is lost.

blocks.subTitle: How do you make a class thread-safe
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: How would you make a class thread-safe?**

First find every critical section — code that reads or writes shared mutable state. Then either guard it with a lock (synchronized method, or a lock around just that section), swap the mutable field for an atomic/thread-safe type, or remove the mutability altogether by making the class immutable.

blocks.subTitle: Thread-safe Singleton
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: How do you make a Singleton thread-safe? What is double-checked locking?**

Eagerly create it at class load (simplest, always thread-safe), synchronize the whole `getInstance()` (correct but slow on every call), or use double-checked locking: check for null, lock, check for null again, then create. DCL keeps the fast path lock-free while still being safe for the one racy first call — but the field must be `volatile` or it can leak a half-built instance.

blocks.subTitle: Why immutability helps concurrency
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Why does immutability help with concurrency?**

A race condition needs shared **mutable** state — if nothing about an object can change after construction, there's no critical section for threads to collide on. Any thread can read an immutable object at any time with zero locking, which is why immutable value objects are the cheapest way to make data thread-safe.

blocks.subTitle: Synchronized method vs double-checked locking
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Why not just synchronize the whole `getInstance()` method — why bother with double-checked locking?**

A fully synchronized method forces every single call, forever, through the lock — even the millionth call, when the instance already exists and no race is possible. DCL's first null-check lets those calls skip the lock entirely, paying the locking cost only during the brief window before the instance first exists.
